I am 72 years old and have worked these North China Plain soils for 55 years. I have seen good years and bad years, and I have learned not to chase every new fad. My household has three people, so labor is limited — my back is not what it used to be, especially when it comes to bending over chili fields for hours.

This year, I will keep **4 mu for winter wheat**. It is already in the ground from last autumn and is greening up now. I use an improved semi-dwarf variety that reliably yields around 1,000 jin per mu. I will top-dress with urea at green-up and irrigate three times: once now, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. I rotary-tilled before sowing last fall.

For **maize**, I plant it on two pieces of land. On the same 4 mu that grows wheat, I will sow **summer maize** immediately after the wheat harvest in early June. I use a no-till planter — there is no reason to plow again when the wheat stubble protects the soil and saves diesel. I also put the remaining **3.1 mu into spring maize**, which I will rotary-till and plant now. In total I have 7.1 mu of maize, all hybrid varieties, which gives me plenty of grain for feed and cash sale.

**Chili** is my cash crop, but I am careful not to plant too much because the spraying and picking are hard on an old man. I keep **3 mu for chili**. I will transplant hybrid *yangjiaohong* seedlings in late April. Chili needs balanced nutrition and steady water from the well, so I apply compound fertilizer and irrigate four times during the hot months. Pests and diseases are the biggest headache — I will spray about 18 times, rotating chemicals so the bugs don't build resistance. I rotary-till the chili plots deeply to break up any pest eggs in the soil.
